title: Asteroid Impact Sparked Firestorms 17 Times Hotter Than Human Lethal Limit
body:
A groundbreaking new study has shed light on the catastrophic events that unfolded in the aftermath of the asteroid impact that led to the demise of the dinosaurs. The research suggests that the massive asteroid collision, which occurred approximately 65 million years ago, may have triggered firestorms with temperatures reaching up to 17 times the thermal limit that is lethal to humans. This apocalyptic scenario would have had a devastating impact on the planet, causing widespread destruction and killing exposed animals within a matter of hours. The findings provide a chilling glimpse into the extreme conditions that prevailed on Earth during one of the most pivotal moments in the planet's history.

The asteroid impact, which is widely believed to have been the primary cause of the mass extinction event that wiped out the dinosaurs, would have thrown up a massive blanket of fine dust into the atmosphere. This dust would have blocked out sunlight, leading to a prolonged period of cold and darkness, known as a "impact winter." However, the new study suggests that this dust may have also had a more immediate and deadly effect. By intensifying a global heat pulse, the dust may have ignited widespread fires, creating firestorms that would have been hot enough to kill any animal that was exposed to them. The sheer scale of the destruction caused by these firestorms would have been unprecedented, and would have played a significant role in the mass extinction event that followed.
